note: Looked at all six at the reference window, and at the eave corners and gable ends at full size. Each reads as a seven-bay timber hall under its roof type: hip_ridge with a main ridge and four hip ridges, hip_gable with a gable over a hip skirt at each end, overhang_gable passing the end columns, flush_gable ending on them, and a long pyramid to one peak. The folded profile curves, steeper toward the ridge, beside the straight one, and every eave turns up at its corners. What a person may dislike: the roof’s purlins and rafter ends draw in the roof’s tile material, not timber, since a roof item takes one material; tile rows on a hip’s end slope run down the slope, as on the base’s hip roof; a gable’s board draws as tiles; and at a risen corner the eave tiles stand a little clear of the rafter ends under them.
